## Report: Acupuncture for Depression During Pregnancy

The evidence supporting acupuncture as a treatment for antenatal depression is **promising but not yet conclusive**.

**Key Trial:** The most significant evidence comes from a randomized controlled trial by Manber et al. (2010), published in *Obstetrics & Gynecology*. In this study, 150 pregnant women meeting DSM-IV criteria for major depressive disorder were randomized to receive either depression-specific acupuncture, non-specific control acupuncture, or prenatal massage over 8 weeks (12 sessions). The researchers found that the short acupuncture protocol demonstrated symptom reduction and a response rate comparable to standard depression treatments, concluding it "could be a viable treatment option for depression during pregnancy" (https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/Abstract/2010/03000/Acupuncture_for_Depression_During_Pregnancy__A.7.aspx).

**Supporting Evidence:** A 2020 pragmatic RCT examining acupuncture as an adjunct intervention for antenatal depression found positive results, though evidence was described as limited to one pilot and one full-powered RCT (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0165032720302081). Researchers noted that while the mechanism remains uncertain, acupuncture may exert effects via the oxytocinergic system (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4758005/).

**Caveats:** A 2013 Cochrane systematic review concluded there was "not enough evidence available to determine if acupuncture" is an effective intervention for antenatal depression (https://www.cochrane.org/th/evidence/CD006795_interventions-other-pharmacological-psychosocial-or-psychological-treating-antenatal-depression). Lead author Rachel Manber herself acknowledged that no universal conclusion exists that acupuncture works for depression, though evidence is growing.

**Conclusion:** The claim is partially supported. One well-designed RCT shows positive results, but the broader systematic review evidence remains insufficient. Acupuncture appears to be a promising option warranting further research.
